Total casualties: 111,306 killed and wounded{{Cite web |url=http://www.nhandan.com.vn/chinhtri/item/7976502-.html |title=Tết Mậu Thân 1968 qua những số liệu – Báo Nhân Dân điện tử |access-date=2018-05-30 |archive-date=2019-04-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190428231454/http://www.nhandan.com.vn/chinhtri/item/7976502-.html |url-status=dead }} }} {{Campaignbox Vietnam War}} The year 1968 saw major developments in the [[Vietnam War]]. The military operations started with an [[New Year's Day Battle of 1968|attack on a US base]] by the [[North Vietnam]]ese [[People's Army of Vietnam]] (PAVN) and the [[Viet Cong]] (VC) on January 1, ending a truce declared by the Pope and agreed upon by all sides. At the end of January, the PAVN and VC launched the [[Tet Offensive]]. [[Hanoi]] erred monumentally in its certainty that the offensive would trigger a supportive uprising of the population. PAVN/VC troops throughout the South, from Hue to the Mekong Delta, attacked in force for the first time in the war, but to devastating cost as the [[Army of the Republic of Vietnam]] (ARVN) and American troops killed close to 37,000 of the ill-supported enemy in less than a month for losses of 3,700 and 7,600 respectively. These reversals on the battlefield (the VC would never again fight effectively as a cohesive force) failed to register on the American home front, however and fueled what would ultimately prove to be a propaganda victory for Hanoi. U.S. troop numbers peaked in 1968 with President Johnson approving an increased maximum number of U.S. troops in Vietnam at 549,500. The year was the most expensive in the Vietnam War with America spending US${{Format price|77350000000}} (US$ {{Format price|{{Inflation|US|77350000000|1968|r=-4}}}} in {{inflation/year|US}}) on the war. The year also became the deadliest of the Vietnam War for America and its allies with 27,915 ARVN soldiers killed and the Americans suffering 16,592 killed compared to around two hundred thousand PAVN/VC killed. The deadliest day of the Vietnam War for the U.S. was 31 January at the start of the Tet Offensive when 246 Americans were killed in action. ==January== ;1–2 January The PAVN violated the New Year's truce in the [[New Year's Day Battle of 1968]]. Among the Americans fighting were future writer [[Larry Heinemann]] and future film director [[Oliver Stone]].{{cite web|date = February 27, 2010|url = http://gaijinass.wordpress.com/2010/02/27/platoon/|title = Platoon: The story of Oliver Stone in Vietnam|publisher = gaijinass|access-date = March 3, 2010|last = Gaijinass|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20100620021713/http://gaijinass.wordpress.com/2010/02/27/platoon/|archive-date = 2010-06-20|url-status = dead}}{{cite book|last=Bates|first=Milton|title=The wars we took to Vietnam: cultural conflict and storytelling|year=1996|publisher = University of California Press|isbn= 978-0-520-20433-1|page=106}} The PAVN lost 328 killed, while U.S. losses were 23 killed.{{cite news|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|title=G.I.'s Kill 348 in Repelling Foe's Attack During Truce|last=Johnson|first=Thomas A.|date=3 January 1968|page=1}} In [[Newsweek]] magazine [[Robert Komer]] touted the early success of the [[Civil Operations and Revolutionary Development Support]] (CORDS) pacification program he led. He said that "only one South Vietnamese in six now lives under VC [Viet Cong] control."{{rp|871}} ;2 January Elements of the [[12th Cavalry Regiment (United States)|12th Cavalry Regiment]] engaged a unit from the PAVN [[2nd Division (Vietnam)|2nd Division]] in a four-hour-long battle 5 km south of [[Firebase Ross]] resulting in 3 U.S. and 39 PAVN killed.{{Rp|99–100}} ;3 January The VC launched more than 50 122 mm rockets at [[Da Nang Air Base]] destroying a [[United States Marine Corps]] (USMC) [[F-4B]] and two [[United States Air Force]] (USAF) aircraft and damaging 17 others.{{cite book|last=Shulimson|first=Jack|title=U.S. Marines in Vietnam: 1968, the Defining Year|publisher=History and Museums Division, USMC|year=1997|url=https://archive.org/stream/USMarinesInVietnamTheDefiningYear1968#page/n0/mode/2up|isbn=0-16-049125-8}}{{PD-notice}}{{rp|98–9}} The PAVN 3rd Regiment, 2nd Division attacked four U.S. firebases in the [[Quế Sơn Valley]] southwest of [[Hội An (city)|Hội An]], launching ground attacks against [[Landing Zone Leslie]] and Firebase Ross. Leslie was occupied by D Company and a platoon from A Company, 2nd Battalion, 12th Cavalry. The PAVN penetrated the base, attacking bunkers with flamethrowers and satchel charges before being pushed out in the afternoon. Losses were 15 U.S and 63 PAVN.{{cite book|last=Krohn|first=Charles|title=The Lost Battalion of Tet: Breakout of the 2/12th Cavalry at Hue|publisher=Naval Institute Press|year=2008|isbn=9781591144342|page=28}} The PAVN emplaced heavy machine guns around Leslie and over a nine-day period shot down seven [[1st Cavalry Division (United States)|1st Cavalry Division]] helicopters and damaged a further 26.{{rp|100}} At Ross the attack was repulsed with losses of 18 U.S. and 331 PAVN killed.{{rp|100}} ;4 January A unit of the U.S. [[4th Infantry Division (United States)|4th Infantry Division]] operating in [[Đắk Tô District]] captured a classified five-page North Vietnamese document, titled "Urgent Combat Order No. 1", that described the strategy for a series of attacks to take place in [[Pleiku]] in conjunction with the upcoming [[Tết]] holiday.{{cite book|last=Willbanks|first=James|title=The Tet Offensive: A Concise History|publisher=Columbia University Press|year=2008|isbn=978-0231128414}}{{rp|28}} A PAVN rocket and mortar attack on [[Ban Me Thuot East Airfield]] destroyed two [[Bell UH-1 Iroquois|UH-1s]] and severely damaged three others.{{cite web|url=https://www.vietnam.ttu.edu/reports/images.php?img=/images/1683/168300010683.pdf|title=Combat After Action Report|publisher=155th Assault Helicopter Company|date=3 February 1968|access-date=14 July 2020}} ;5 January The "Boston Five" [[Michael Ferber]], [[Dr. Benjamin Spock]], [[William Sloan Coffin]], [[Mitchell Goodman]] and [[Marcus Raskin]] were indicted by a [[Grand jury]] in [[Boston]] on charges of conspiring to counsel young men to violate [[Conscription in the United States|draft]] laws.{{cite news|title=Boston Grand Jury Indicts Five For Working Against Draft crashed in the [[Hải Lăng District|Hải Lăng Forest]] south of [[Đông Hà Combat Base]], killing all 46 personnel on board{{cite web|url=https://aviation-safety.net/wikibase/wiki.php?id=76027|title=ASN Wikibase Occurrence #76027|publisher=Aviation Safety Network|access-date=20 August 2020}} ;9 January At a meeting with Commander of the [[Military Assistance Command, Vietnam]] (MACV) General [[William Westmoreland]], [[II Field Force, Vietnam]] commander [[Major general (United States)|Major General]] [[Frederick C. Weyand]] showed Westmoreland that PAVN/VC main force units in the [[III Corps (South Vietnam)|III Corps]] area were moving in from the [[Cambodia]]n border towards [[Saigon]]. Weyand received permission from Westmoreland to cancel scheduled operations near the border and shift his forces back towards Saigon.{{cite book|last=Cosmas|first=Graham|title=The Joint Chiefs of Staff and The War in Vietnam 1960–1968 Part 3|publisher=Office of Joint History Office of the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff|year=2009|url=https://www.jcs.mil/Portals/36/Documents/History/Vietnam/Vietnam_1960-1968_P003.pdf|isbn=978-1482378696}}{{PD-notice}}{{rp|144}} ;10 January VC sappers penetrate the perimeter of [[Kontum Airfield]] and destroyed several helicopters with [[Satchel charge]]s, killing 7 Americans and wounding 25. An estimated 16 VC were killed in the attack.{{cite news|title=Vietcong Press Drive From Highlands to Delta; Base and Towns Shelled -Civilian Deaths Reported|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1968/01/11/archives/vietcong-press-drive-from-highlands-to-delta-base-and-towns-shelled.html|date=11 January 1968|access-date=14 July 2020}} ;12 January The [[Kampuchean Revolutionary Army]] was established by the orders of [[Pol Pot]], the leader of the [[Communist Party of Kampuchea]] (CPK).{{cite book|last=Bartrop|first=Paul|title=A Biographical Encyclopedia of Contemporary Genocide: Portraits of Evil and Good|publisher=ABC-CLIO|year=2012|isbn=978-0313386787|page=122}} ;15 January to 9 February Operation San Angelo was a 1st Brigade, [[101st Airborne Division]] search and destroy operation in [[Đắk Nông Province|Quang Duc]] and [[Phước Long Province]]s. the operation resulted in 63 PAVN/VC and 12 U.S. killed.{{cite web|url=https://www.vietnam.ttu.edu/resources/operations/operations.txt|title=Vietnam Archive Operations Database|publisher=The Vietnam Center and Archive|accessdate=10 November 2021}} ;18 January [[File:Clark M. Clifford.jpg|thumb|right|Clark Clifford and General Earle Wheeler]] [[President of the United States|President]] [[Lyndon Johnson]] nominates [[Clark Clifford]] to succeed [[Robert McNamara]] as [[United States Secretary of Defense]].{{cite book|author=Roger R. Trask|title=The Secretaries of Defense: A Brief History, 1947–1985|url=https://archive.org/details/secretariesofdef00wash|year=1985|publisher=Historical Office, Office of the Secretary of Defense|page=[https://archive.org/details/secretariesofdef00wash/page/34 34]}} At a [[White House]] luncheon with First Lady [[Lady Bird Johnson]] in a discussion about juvenile delinquency, singer [[Eartha Kitt]] said "You send the best of this country off to be shot and maimed. They rebel in the street. They will take pot ... and they will get high. They don't want to go to school because they're going to be snatched off from their mothers to be shot in Vietnam." Her remarks caused Mrs. Johnson to burst into tears and led to Kitt being blacklisted and investigated by the CIA, effectively ending her career.{{cite news|title='Sex kitten' vs. Lady Bird: The day Eartha Kitt attacked the Vietnam War at the White House|author=DeNeen L. Brown|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=19 January 2018|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/retropolis/wp/2018/01/19/sex-kitten-vs-first-lady-eartha-kitt-yells-at-lady-bird-johnson-about-vietnam/}} ;19 January In the first two weeks of 1968, PAVN/VC forces shelled 49 district and provincial capitals in [[South Vietnam]] and temporarily occupied two of them. General Westmoreland described the fighting to ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' magazine "as the most intense of the entire war." MACV claimed that 5,000 PAVN/VC had been killed.{{rp|896}} ;20 January [[Ron Kovic]] serving with the [[1st Amphibian Tractor Battalion]], [[3rd Marine Division]] was shot and paralysed during a battle with the PAVN in the vicinity of the village of My Loc, in the [[Demilitarized Zone (Vietnam)|Demilitarized Zone]] (DMZ).{{cite book|last=Gay|first=Kathlyn|title=American Dissidents: An Encyclopedia of Activists, Subversives, and Prisoners of Conscience|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZzQVpPvlVMcC&pg=PA362|year=2012|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=978-1-59884-764-2|pages=359–362}} ;20–31 January 1969 [[Operation McLain]] a security operation conducted by the U.S. 3rd Battalion, [[506th Infantry Regiment]], 101st Airborne Division and ARVN 44th Regiment, [[23rd Division (South Vietnam)|23rd Division]] in [[Bình Thuận Province]] commences. The operation results in 1,042 VC and 69 U.S. killed.{{cite book|last=Villard|first=Erik|title=United States Army in Vietnam Combat Operations Staying the Course October 1967 to September 1968|publisher=Center of Military History United States Army|year=2017|isbn=9780160942808|url=https://history.army.mil/html/books/091/91-15-1/index.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180206190325/https://history.army.mil/html/books/091/91-15-1/index.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 6, 2018}}{{PD-notice}}{{rp|478}}{{cite web|url=https://apps.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/a955261.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200226032528/https://apps.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/a955261.pdf|url-status=live|archive-date=February 26, 2020|title=United States Military Assistance Command, Vietnam Command History 1969 Volume III|publisher=Headquarters United States Military Assistance Command, Vietnam|date=30 April 1970|access-date=5 July 2020|page=L-3}}{{PD-notice}} ;21 January [[North Korea]]n [[Unit 124|commandos]] carry out the [[Blue House raid]], the most significant escalation in the [[Korean DMZ Conflict|low-intensity conflict]] that had been underway in [[South Korea]] since October 1966. The attack raised the possibility that the South Korean Government might want to withdraw some of their forces in South Vietnam for homeland defense, requiring their replacement by already overstretched American forces.{{rp|152}} ;21 January – 31 March [[Operation Jeb Stuart]] was planned as an operation by the 1st Cavalry Division to attack PAVN base areas in I Corps, but instead saw the division supporting other Allied forces during the Tet Offensive.{{rp|16}} ;21 January – 9 July [[File:C-130 Hercules taking off from Khe Sanh 1968.jpg|thumb|right|A C-130 takes off from Khe Sanh]] The long and bloody [[Battle of Khe Sanh]] began with an assault by the PAVN on [[Khe Sanh Combat Base]] in northwestern Quảng Trị Province. The combatants were elements of the U.S. [[III Marine Amphibious Force]] (III MAF) and the ARVN against two to three PAVN division-size elements.Clarke, Bruce B. G. (2007), ''Expendable warriors: the Battle of Khe Sanh and the Vietnam War'', Greenwood Publishing Group, p. 69 PAVN General [[Võ Nguyên Giáp]] later claimed that his objective was to create a diversion to draw U.S. forces away from the populated areas of South Vietnam. Khe Sanh diverted 30,000 US troops away from the cities that would be the main targets of the Tet Offensive.Page, Tim and Pimlott, John Pimlott (1990), ''Nam – The Vietnam Experience, 1965–75'', London: Hamlyn, p. 324 The USAF began [[Operation Niagara]] to provide continuous air support during the siege.{{cite book|last=Nalty|first=Bernard|title=Air Power and the Fight for Khe Sanh|publisher=Office of Air Force History|year=1986|isbn=9781508416906|url=https://media.defense.gov/2010/May/26/2001330289/-1/-1/0/AFD-100526-029.pdf|page=95}} ;21 January - 23 November [[Operation Lancaster II]] a security operation to keep [[National Route 9 (Vietnam)|Route 9]] open to [[Ca Lu Combat Base]] in northern [[Quảng Trị Province]] commences. By the end of the operation the Marines had lost 359 killed; PAVN fatalities were estimated to be in excess of 1,800.{{rp|119}} ;23 January North Korean forces seize the {{USS|Pueblo|AGER-2|6}}.{{rp|152}} ;23–4 January The [[Battle of Ban Houei Sane]] began on the night of 23 January, when the 24th Regiment of the PAVN [[304th Division (Vietnam)|304th Division]] overran the small [[Royal Lao Army]] (RLA) outpost at Ban Houei Sane. The PAVN lost 29 killed, while RLA losses are unknown. The RLA survivors fled across the border to Lang Vei Special Forces Camp.{{cite book|last=Cash|first=John|title= Seven Firefights in Vietnam|year=1985|publisher=DIANE Publishing|isbn=978-1-56806-563-2|page=111}} ;23 January - 12 February [[Operation Coronado X]] conducted by the U.S. [[Mobile Riverine Force]] (MRF) and the ARVN, was originally planned as a sweep of western [[Dinh Tuong Province]] and eastern [[Kien Phong Province]], however with the outbreak of the [[Tet Offensive]] on 31 January 1968 it instead became the MRF reaction to eject VC forces from [[Mỹ Tho province|Mỹ Tho]] and [[Vĩnh Long province|Vĩnh Long]]. The operation resulted in 269 VC killed for the loss of 12 U.S. killed.{{cite book|last=Fulton|first=William B.|title=Riverine Operations 1966–1969|publisher=[[United States Army Center of Military History]]|url= https://archive.org/details/CMHPub90-18/page/n1|year=1973|isbn=978-1780392479}}{{PD-notice}}{{rp|148}} ;24 January − 1 March [[File:W Coy 2RARNZ during Operation Coburg SVN 1968 (AWM CAM680180VN).jpg|thumb|right|W Coy 2RARNZ patrol during Operation Coburg]] [[Operation Coburg]] was an Australian military action that saw heavy fighting between the [[1st Australian Task Force]] (1ATF) and PAVN and VC forces during the wider fighting around [[Long Binh Post|Long Binh]] and [[Biên Hòa]].{{cite book|last1=McNeill|first1=Ian|last2=Ekins|first2=Ashley|title=On the offensive: the Australian Army in the Vietnam War, January 1967 – June 1968|year=2003|publisher=Allen & Unwin|isbn= 978-1-86373-304-5|page=290}} ;26 January In ''Time'' magazine, General Westmoreland said, "the Communists seem to have run temporarily out of steam."{{rp|896}} Two companies of the PAVN 408th Sapper Battalion attacked [[Camp Holloway]] destroying five UH-1 helicopters and an ammunition storage area.{{cite web|url=https://www.vietnam.ttu.edu/reports/images.php?img=/images/1683/168300010691.pdf|title=Enemy Attack on US Installations After Action Report|publisher=Headquarters 52nd Combat Aviation Battalion|date=31 January 1968|access-date=14 July 2020}} ;28 January General Westmoreland in his annual report said "In many areas the enemy has been driven away from the population centers; in others he has been compelled to disperse and evade contact thus nullifying much of his potential. The year ended with the enemy increasingly resorting to desperation tactics in attempting to achieve military/psychological victory; and he has experienced only failure in those attempts."{{rp|872}} ;January – February 1973 [[Operation Igloo White]] was a covert U.S. military electronic warfare operation carried out by the USAF [[553d Reconnaissance Wing]] and the [[United States Navy]] [[VO-67]] squadron to detect and interdict the Ho Chi Minh Trail.{{cite book|last=Van Staaveren|first=Jacob|title=Interdiction in Southern Laos, 1961–1968|publisher=Center of Air Force History|year=1993|url=https://media.defense.gov/2010/Sep/27/2001329814/-1/-1/0/AFD-100927-078.pdf|isbn=978-1410220608}}{{PD-notice}}{{rp|255}} ===Tet Offensive=== [[File:DeadVietCong1968.jpg|thumb|Viet Cong soldier killed during the [[Tet Offensive attack on US Embassy]]]] ;29 January At half-past midnight on Wednesday morning the PAVN launch the Tet Offensive at [[Nha Trang]]. At 2:45 that morning the [[Embassy of the United States, Saigon|US Embassy]] in Saigon is [[Tet Offensive attack on US Embassy|attacked]], the VC fail to enter the Embassy building and 18 are killed and one captured, U.S. losses are five killed.{{rp|34–6}} ;29–30 January The VC fired rockets at Da Nang Air Base and then at 02:30 on 30 January they launched a sapper and mortar attack on the south of the base killing four Marines. At 03:30 a renewed rocket attack on the base began with 55 122 mm rockets hitting within 20 minutes, killing three marines and wounding 11 and destroying five aircraft and damaging a further 14.{{rp|145–8}} ;30 January-4 February The PAVN 406th Sapper Battalion and a company from the VC 304th Local Force Battalion attacked Kontum Airfield but were forced back by U.S. helicopter gunships and armor. The PAVN renewed their attack but failed to penetrate the airfield defenses. On 31 January, Company D, 1st Battalion, [[22nd Infantry Regiment (United States)|22nd Infantry Regiment]] was landed at the airfield and the next day two companies from the 1st Battalion, [[12th Infantry Regiment (United States)|12th Infantry Regiment]] were flown into the airfield securing its northern perimeter. By 4 February the city had been secured and normal operations resumed at the airfield.{{rp|302–7}} ;30 January – 3 March [[File:OperationHueCity1967wounded.jpg|thumb|right|Marine wounded in the Battle of Huế]] The [[Battle of Huế]] was one of the bloodiest and longest battles. The ARVN and three understrength U.S. Marine [[battalion]]s attacked and defeated more than 10,000 entrenched PAVN/VC.{{cite book |last=Stanton|first=Shelby|title=Vietnam order of battle|year=2003|publisher=Stackpole Books|isbn=978-0-8117-0071-9}}{{rp|11}} The PAVN/VC lost 5,113 killed and 98 captured in the battle, the ARVN lost 452 killed and the U.S. 216 killed.{{rp|213}} 844 Civilians were killed in the fighting. In the [[Massacre at Huế]] the PAVN/VC massacred 2,800–6,000 civilians and prisoners of war during their occupation of the city.{{cite book|last=Anderson|first=David|title=The Columbia Guide to the Vietnam War|publisher=Columbia University Press|year=2004|isbn=978-0231114936|pages=98–9}} In the aftermath of the battle South Vietnamese forces killed an estimated 1,000-2,000 people suspected of being VC or VC sympathisers. ;31 January In the deadliest single day for U.S. forces during the war 246 Americans were killed.{{cite news|title=The men killed on a single, bloody day in Vietnam, and the haunting wall that memorializes them|newspaper=The Washington Post|author=Joel Achenbach|date=25 May 2018|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/retropolis/wp/2018/05/25/the-men-killed-on-a-single-day-in-the-vietnam-war-and-the-haunting-wall-that-memorializes-them/}} ;31 January – 7 March loss of 22 U.S. and 29 ARVN.{{cite book|last=Nolan|first=Keith|title=The Battle for Saigon Tet 1968|publisher=Presidio Press|year=1996|isbn=0891417699}}{{rp|92}} In the [[Tet Offensive attack on Joint PAVN/VC lost 914 killed and 86 captured.{{cite book|last=Rawson|first=Andrew|title=Battle Story Tet Offensive 1968|publisher=The History Press|year=2013|isbn=9780752492506|page=16}} A VC rocket and RLA losses were 300 killed and 400 missing while PAVN/Pathet Lao losses are unknown.{{cite book|last1=Conboy|first1=Kenneth|last2=Morrison|first2=James|title=Shadow War: The CIA's Secret War in Laos|publisher=Paladin Press|year=1996|isbn=0-87364-825-0}}{{rp|201–5}} ;28 November North Vietnam announced that it would negotiate only with the United States, or refuse to attend the talks altogether.{{cite news|title=Hanoi Snubs Saigon Regime In Paris Talks|newspaper=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette|date=29 November 1968|page=1}} ;29 November Radio Hanoi broadcast a VC directive for a new offensive to "utterly destroy" Allied forces, particularly the Phoenix Program units.{{rp|279–80}} ==December== ;December to 11 May 1969 [[Operation Speedy Express]] a controversial United States military operation conducted in the Mekong Delta provinces of [[Kien Hoa]] and Vĩnh Bình begins. The operation was launched to prevent VC units from interfering with pacification efforts and to interdict lines of communication and deny them the use of base areas.{{rp|12}} ;3 December – 19 February 1969 [[File:Australian soldier during Operation Goodwood (1968-1969).jpg|thumb|right|An Australian soldier inspects a VC bunker]] In the [[Battle of Hat Dich]] 1ATF and ARVN forces engaged PAVN/VC units in the [[Hat Dich]] Secret Zone, [[Hắc Dịch]]. The battle resulted in 245 PAVN/VC killed and 17 captured and 22 Australians/New Zealanders and 31 ARVN killed.{{cite book|last=Avery|first=Brian|title=In the ANZAC Spirit: The Fourth Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment/NZ (ANZAC): South Vietnam 1968 to 1969|publisher=Slouch Hat Publications|year=2002|isbn=0-95797521X|page=155}} ;8 December - 10 February 1969 Operation Le Loi I was a security operation conducted by the ARVN 1st Ranger Group in Quảng Nam Province. The operation resulted in 695 PAVN/VC killed.{{rp|280}} ;9 December to 28 February 1969 Operation Marshall Mountain was a 1st Brigade, 5th Infantry Division (Mechanized) and ARVN 1st Regiment, 1st Division clear and search operation in eastern Quảng Trị Province. The operation resulted in 78 PAVN and six U.S. killed. ;12 December – 9 March 1969 [[Operation Taylor Common]] was a [[search and destroy]] operation conducted by ''Task Force Yankee'', a task organized force of the 1st Marine Division. The objective was to clear the An Hoa Basin, neutralize the PAVN's Base Area 112 and develop Fire Support Bases (FSBs) to interdict PAVN infiltration routes leading from the Laotian border.{{rp|12}} The operation resulted in 1,398 PAVN killed and 29 captured and 183 Marines and 100 ARVN killed.{{rp|94}} ;15 December Clifford states that the U.S. has no obligation to maintain current force levels in South Vietnam and that U.S. and North Vietnamese forces can be withdrawn as talks progress.{{rp|281}} ;15 December to 5 January 1969 Operation Valiant Hunt was a BLT [[2nd Battalion, 26th Marines]] and [[HMM-362]] clear and search operation on Barrier Island, south of Hội An. the operation resulted in 33 PAVN/VC and three Marines killed.{{rp|300}} ;15 December to 28 February 1969 [[Operation Fayette Canyon]] was a security operation conducted by the 196th Infantry Brigade in "Antenna Valley", [[Hiệp Đức District]] and in the Nui Mat Rang mountains northwest of Tam Kỳ. The operation resulted in 327 PAVN/VC killed and four captured and two U.S. killed.{{cite web|url=https://www.vietnam.ttu.edu/reports/images.php?img=/images/107/1070204004.pdf|title=Weekly Summary|publisher=Headquarters United States Military Assistance Command, Vietnam office of Information|date=23 January 1969|access-date=5 July 2020}}{{PD-notice}} ;17 December Democratic senator George McGovern described Kỳ as a "little tinhorn dictator" in comments that Saigon was delaying the peace negotiations.{{rp|281}} ;18 December Writing in ''Foreign Affairs'' Henry Kissinger proposed twin track negotiations with the U.S. and North Vietnam agreeing a mutual de-escalation and South Vietnam and the VC agreeing a political settlement.
